info.disambiguation: English singer, songwriter, pianist, and composer
info.bio:
Sir Elton Hercules John (n. Pinner, Inglaterra; 25 de marzo de 1947), es un cantante, compositor y pianista británico de música pop y rock, nacido como Reginald Kenneth Dwight Harris.

A lo largo de sus más de 40 años de carrera musical, Elton John ha vendido más de 250 millones de discos y ha colocado más de 50 canciones en las listas de éxitos, convirtiéndose en uno de los mejores músicos de todos los tiempos. En el año 2004 la revista Rolling Stone le otorgó el puesto 49 en su lista de los 100 mejores artistas de la historia.

scenes.name: Los funky setenta: Soul Train y el estilo negro
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Entre 1972 y 1976 la comunidad negra cambió más que nunca, pero fuera de los telediarios: los líderes radicales, en los tribunales; la revolución, convertida en estilo; «Power to the people» en 1972 y «Have a nice day» en 1976. La cultura negra se volvió nacional: «hermano» y «hermana», el saludo de cinco, «Right on», afros, plataformas, dashikis, astrología y marihuana; Sly, Angela Davis o Tina Turner como embajadores del estilo y bailes nuevos (el robot, el penguin) extendidos por la televisión. Lo funky, palabrota en los sesenta, se volvió «baaad»: tras «Ain’t It Funky» y «Funky Drummer» llegaron el «Funky Chicken», el «Funky Worm», el «Funky Nassau» o «Funky Music Sho Nuff Turns Me On». La tele pasó de I Spy a The Flip Wilson Show y Sanford and Son, con el cómico guarro Redd Foxx. Soul Train, de Don Cornelius (exmarine y DJ de Chicago, financiado por Sears y Afro Sheen), fue la meca del decenio: la sexualidad negra sin diluir cada sábado por la mañana; Elton John fue el primer blanco en actuar. Los Dells cantaron «The Origin of Funk» («ahora que lo hemos recuperado») e Ishmael Reed imaginó en Mumbo Jumbo (1972) el «Jes Grew», una antiplaga rítmica negra que contagia a América, fuente de inspiración de Clinton. Era la transformación final: el amor propio total, ser funky y orgulloso.

scenes.name: Cantautores de los setenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: James Taylor se convierte, misteriosamente, en el prototipo del cantautor de los setenta; Carole King, Carly Simon y Don McLean, sobrevalorados. Las innovaciones llegan del oeste: Randy Newman y sus viñetas urbanas con fusión de estilos populares, Shawn Phillips, J.J. Cale y su estilo «laid-back», Gram Parsons, Emmylou Harris, Roger McGuinn, Jackson Browne (Late For The Sky) y, sobre todo, Tom Waits, discípulo de Beefheart y cronista de marginados (Swordfishtrombones, Rain Dogs). Excéntricos como Todd Rundgren y Annette Peacock; en Gran Bretaña, Peter Hammill, Anthony Moore, Richard Thompson, Robert Calvert, John Cale, Kevin Coyne, Elton John y los ex Beatles. El realismo de Bruce Springsteen, verdadero heredero de Woody Guthrie y del blues, y la escuela italiana de cantautores (De André, Guccini, Battisti, Sorrenti).

scenes.name: 2000: apogeo y caída de la industria
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Los noventa ven el apogeo y la caída de la industria discográfica: el CD multiplica sus ingresos (cinco «majors» controlan el 95% de los discos vendidos en 1999), Mariah Carey bate récords de Presley y los Beatles y «Candle In The Wind» de Elton John supera a «White Christmas» como canción más vendida. Pero en 1999 Shawn Fanning funda Napster y millones de internautas dejan de pagar por la música: en 2001 las ventas caen por primera vez en años.

podcast.title: American Debut at The Troubadour (September 12, 1970)
podcast.body: Elton John made his pivotal American debut at The Troubadour on September 12, 1970, introduced by Neil Diamond. The club was packed with record executives eager to find the next big star. Reflecting on Doug Weston's death in 1999, Elton John stated that his "whole life came alive that night, musically, emotionally, everything," transforming him from a fan to an accepted musician and turning him into a star within a week in Los Angeles. "My whole life came alive that night, musically, emotionally, everything. It was like everything I had been waiting for suddenly happened."

podcast.title: Gorilla Suit Stage Crash (1973)
podcast.body: In October 1973, Elton John, intending to prank David Bowie and potentially sign The Stooges, donned a rented gorilla suit and bounded onto the stage during a Stooges performance at Richard's Club in Atlanta. He surprised an already drug-addled Iggy Pop, who mistook him for a real gorilla, and nearly got into a fight with James Williamson before revealing his identity. "Elton John dressed in a gorilla suit, bounds on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Pinball Wizard" Film Role (1975)
podcast.body: Elton John reportedly agreed to play the Pinball Wizard in the 1975 movie version of *Tommy* and cover the song under the condition that he could keep the enormous boots, which made him appear approximately ten feet tall. In the film, his character's instrument was a pinball machine integrated with a keyboard, and he wore his characteristic sparkly glasses, a sparkly beanie topped with a pinball, and the signature boots, perfectly embodying the 1975 aesthetic. "Elton reportedly agreed to play the pinball wizard and cover the song if he could keep the enormous boots that made him about 10 feet tall."

podcast.title: Significant Income from Residencies and Broadway (2016)
podcast.body: Elton John ranked between positions 26 and 27, earning around 60 million dollars, despite appearing to release little new material. A major source of his income came from nearly 100 concerts performed in Las Vegas, which are described as possibly the most profitable concerts globally. He also earns substantial income from musical production for Broadway musicals and is currently working on a new Broadway musical project. "ha hecho un casi 100 conciertos en las Vegas, que son posiblemente los conciertos más rentables que hay en el mundo."

podcast.body: Elton John's life was depicted in the movie "Rocketman," which grossed $200 million. This film is an example of the popular music biopic trend that has been prominent over the last two decades. "If Bohemian Rhapsody can make a billion dollars and Rocket Man can bring in 200 million, studios are going to want to make more of these things."

podcast.body: Elton John's flamboyant persona was accepted by mainstream audiences because it was perceived as "theater" or "performance," allowing audiences to enjoy his music without confronting his personal life. "Straight suburbia did not really want to know what Liberachi or Bowie or Elton John were doing in their bedrooms."

podcast.title: Attempt to Sign Iggy Pop (early 1970s)
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, after establishing his own record label, Elton John sought to sign Iggy Pop. He attended an Iggy gig in Atlanta, where he planned a surprise by dressing in a gorilla costume and joining Iggy on stage. "Elton flew to an Iggy gig in Atlanta where for some reason Elton John decided to surprise Iggy by dressing up in a gorilla costume and joining Iggy on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Critical Acclaim from Robert Hilburn
podcast.body: Robert Hilburn, music critic for the Los Angeles Times, attended Elton John's American debut at The Troubadour and immediately announced the arrival of a new rock star. Hilburn praised John's originality, noting that his "crazy outfit was his only showbiz flair," with the rest being "music industry business," and welcomed him as a "new bit of magic" during a period Hilburn considered unproductive for new talent in rock. "Hillburn announced that there was a new rock star in town."

podcast.title: Defining Classic Rock in Early 1990s
podcast.body: Elton John was recognized as an older act that helped define the category of "classic rock" in the early 1990s, a period when the musical landscape was shifting away from the excesses of hair metal. "Rock was dominated by hair metal bands, which was really starting to get old and played out. It was also dominated by older acts that were defining a new term, classic rock, Rolling Stones, Pink Floyd, Elton John, and so on."

podcast.body: Elton John's concert tours have exceeded the gross revenue of U2's 360 tour, positioning him among the highest-earning artists in modern live music. "Ed Sheeran, Elton John, Coldplay, and Taylor Swift have eclipsed that."

podcast.body: Elton John acts as Eminem's sponsor in Alcoholics Anonymous, providing support and understanding from his own experience with addiction. Eminem contacts him when he needs strength. podcast.body: Despite his dramatic stage appearance in a gorilla suit, Elton John's mutual admiration with Iggy Pop and The Stooges did not result in him signing the band to a record contract. "Elton never did sign him or the band to a record contract."

podcast.title: Fats Domino Tribute
podcast.body: Elton John participated in the recording of a tribute album for Fats Domino, joining other major artists to raise funds for rebuilding Domino's home after its destruction by Hurricane Katrina, showcasing widespread admiration for Domino. "everyone from Elton John to Dr. John, from Paul McCartney to Robert Plant, will come together to record a tribute album to help raise funds to rebuild it."

podcast.title: Friendship with Billie Jean King
podcast.body: Elton John met tennis legend Billie Jean King at Wimbledon in 1974, leading to a close friendship where they became "each other's groupies." They bonded over tennis, playing mixed doubles in an exhibition match before a Philadelphia Freedoms game, and likely shared a common ground in their challenges regarding public declarations of their sexual orientation. Elton John also participated in a two-week tennis camp at John Gardener's tennis ranch in Paradise Valley, Arizona, alongside celebrities like Johnny Carson and Clint Eastwood. "Elton John met Billy Jean King at Wimbledon in 1974 and they kind of became each other's groupies."

podcast.title: Immediate Post-Debut Success
podcast.body: Following his electrifying first show at The Troubadour, Bill Graham, the owner of the Filmore East in New York, offered Elton John $5,000 to perform there. This amount was a significant endorsement, as it was more than Graham had ever offered a new artist before. "After his first show at the Trubidor, Bill Graham, the owner of the Philmore East in New York, offered Elton John $5,000 to perform there, which is more than he had ever offered a new artist before."

podcast.title: John Wayne Gacy's Musical Preference
podcast.body: Serial killer John Wayne Gacy, responsible for at least 33 victims, was noted to be a fan of Elton John, among other artists. This detail highlights his personal musical tastes despite his horrific crimes. "John Wayne Gacy... was into Elton John, Bob Dylan, Neil Diamond, and Aureo Speedwagon."

podcast.body: Kiki Dee, who provided background vocals on Elton John's 1973 Christmas song "Step into Christmas," later had a hit duet with Elton John titled "Don't Go Breaking My Heart" in 1976. "Elton John fans will recall that Elton had a hit duet, don't go break in my heart with Kiki D in 1976 while she was singing background on that song."

podcast.title: Leading Activist for LGBTQ+ Rights
podcast.body: As an openly declared homosexual, Elton John has been a crucial figure for the rights of homosexual communities, not only through his musical work but significantly through his activism. He founded numerous support groups for homosexual rights, advocated for same-sex marriage, and conducted many political campaigns. He is one of the most committed artists as an activist, having donated and raised substantial funds for sexual freedom causes. "Él ha fundado muchísimos grupos de apoyo a los derechos de los homosexuales para apoyar el matrimonio homosexual, ha incluso hecho muchísimas campañas políticas a favor de los derechos."

podcast.title: Major International Rock Act (Early 1970s)
podcast.body: Elton John was one of the biggest international rock acts in the early 1970s, at a time when much of rock music was considered tired. "The biggest international rock acts in the early 1970s were Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd, The Rolling Stones, Elton John, and as unbelievable as it sounds today, Grand Funk Railroad."

podcast.title: Managed by John Reid
podcast.body: Elton John was managed by John Reid, who also looked after Queen. Reid's role involved handling the careers of two of music's most flamboyant and successful acts, a task described as likely "a handful."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Massive Career Based on Piano Songs
podcast.body: Elton John established a massive career, largely built upon his piano-centric songs. He is cited as a prime example of an artist whose primary instrument and songwriting approach centered around the piano, leading to significant commercial success. "We do have Elton John and Billy Joel and Carol King. They all had massive careers based largely on piano songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Tribute to Philadelphia Sound
podcast.body: Elton John, with Bernie Taupin, crafted "Philadelphia Freedom" not just as a tribute to Billie Jean King's tennis team, but deliberately in the style of the "Philadelphia sound." He explicitly stated his intention for it to be a tribute to "black music" and to sound like a "funky black record," aiming for it to cross over into the "black market" of music. The song incorporates R&B elements and lush strings to achieve this desired sound. "Elton said it is and I quote, black music. He said, I wanted the record to be a tribute to music that I like."

podcast.title: Rivalry with David Bowie
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, Elton John was in a friendly competition with his friend David Bowie over who could be the biggest British rock star. Bowie was also friends with Iggy Pop and working with The Stooges, influencing Elton's desire to prank Bowie and potentially sign The Stooges. concerts.title: Soul Train Appearance (1975)
concerts.body: Elton John appeared on Soul Train just months before David Bowie's November 1975 appearance, making him one of the first white performers on the televised dance show hosted by Don Cornelius. "Boey was among the first white performers on the show, just months after Elton John had appeared."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Elton John Gorilla Incident (1973)
xref.body: In October 1973, while the Stooges were on a punishing tour and Iggy was heavily incapacitated by Quaaludes, Elton John—dressed in a rented gorilla suit—surprised Iggy on stage at Richard's Club in Atlanta as part of a prank and a potential move to sign the band. Iggy, hallucinating, freaked out believing it was a real gorilla, and the band's guitarist James Williamson almost attacked Elton before his identity was revealed. "Elton John dressed in a gorilla suit, bounds on stage. Iggy, in his altered state and seeing triple, freaked out, thinking that this was a real gorilla."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Elton John Gorilla Suit Incident – Richards, Atlanta, October 1973
xref.body: In October 1973, Iggy Pop and the Stooges were playing at Richards in Atlanta at the same time Elton John was touring America. Elton — engaged in a semi-friendly rivalry with David Bowie, who was a known Stooges supporter — decided to crash the show dressed in a full gorilla suit to surprise Iggy on stage. A photographer from Detroit music magazine *Creem* was tipped off. No one warned Iggy that this was planned, and no one warned Elton that Iggy was heavily intoxicated on speed that night. When Elton bounded onto the stage in the gorilla suit, Iggy genuinely believed it was a real gorilla, was terrified, and fled the stage. The incident was captured on film. After Elton removed the gorilla head and multiple people calmed Iggy down, the show resumed and the two performed several songs together — Iggy bare-chested, Elton still in the suit. "Iggy thought it was an actual gorilla. And this freak out is captured on film."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Elton John's Attempted Signing and Gorilla Prank (1973)
xref.body: Elton John, in a competitive rivalry with David Bowie, attempted to show support for and potentially sign The Stooges to his new record label. This led to a surprise visit where Elton, in a gorilla suit, crashed their stage in October 1973, startling Iggy Pop who was heavily under the influence of Quaaludes. "Elton thought he'd have a little fun with Bowie and his relationship with the Stooges, and in the process, maybe he could sign them to his new record label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Percussionist for "Live and Let Die" (1973)
xref.body: Ray Cooper, a renowned percussionist who has collaborated with a wide range of artists including Elton John, Pink Floyd, and Eric Clapton, played percussion on Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" theme. His involvement brought a significant rhythmic element to the globally successful rock song. "The percussionist on that song is Ray Cooper who has worked with everyone from Elton John to Pink Floyd to Eric Clapton."

xref.title: Defining Classic Rock in Early 1990s
xref.body: In the early 1990s, as hair metal was becoming played out, the Rolling Stones were among the older acts that began to define the new term "classic rock," showcasing their enduring appeal alongside contemporary genres. "Rock was dominated by hair metal bands, which was really starting to get old and played out. It was also dominated by older acts that were defining a new term, classic rock, Rolling Stones, Pink Floyd, Elton John, and so on."

xref.title: Notable Clients and Albums
xref.body: Over its decade of operation, AIR Montserrat hosted many major artists, including Bush, Elton John, Supertramp, The Rolling Stones, Pink Floyd, Duran Duran, Black Sabbath, Paul McCartney, and Dire Straits. Albums like *Brothers in Arms*, *Ghosts in the Machine*, and *Synchronicity* were recorded there. "Bush, Elton Johns, Super Tramp, The Rolling Stones, Pink Floyd, Durand Durand, Black Sabbath, Paul McCartney, Dire Straits, they all went to Air Studios Montserrat."

xref.title: Unexpected Piano Acquisition and Early Influences
xref.body: Ben Folds' musical journey began at age nine when his carpenter father accepted a piano as payment from a customer unable to pay for a job. This serendipitous event allowed Ben to become a fan of Elton John and Billy Joel, prompting him to learn their songs by ear from the radio. "The best thing that ever happened to Ben was when his father brought home a piano. He was a carpenter where the customer couldn't pay for a job, so he was paid with a piano. This was perfect for nine-year-old Ben because he'd become a fan of Elton John and Billy Joel and began learning songs off the radio."
